name: Banded Squat Walk
description: The banded squat walk is a dynamic hip abduction exercise performed in a partial squat position while stepping laterally against the resistance of a loop band placed above the knees or around the ankles. Maintaining a squat while stepping sideways forces the gluteus medius to both stabilize the pelvis and drive abduction, making it an effective warm-up and accessory exercise for lower body training.

execution.starting_position: Place a loop resistance band above the knees (easier) or around the ankles (harder). Stand with feet shoulder-width apart and descend into a partial squat — roughly quarter to half squat depth.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose band tension based on ability. Heavier bands around the knees provide more resistance; lighter bands around the ankles increase range.
steps: Step 1: Place the band above knees or around ankles. Assume a partial squat with feet shoulder-width apart, chest up, core braced.
Step 2: Step one foot laterally to widen the stance beyond shoulder width, maintaining the squat depth.
Step 3: Bring the trailing foot to follow, returning to shoulder-width stance — still in squat.
Step 4: Continue walking in the same direction for the prescribed distance or steps.
Step 5: Repeat in the opposite direction.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe rhythmically throughout — exhale with each step.
common_mistakes: Standing up out of the squat between steps — maintain depth throughout
Letting the knees cave inward — push knees out against the band
Taking too large a step, which compromises squat position
safety_considerations: Low risk exercise; common as a warm-up before squats and deadlifts
Avoid if the band causes knee pain — use a lighter band or adjust position
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Steps of 30–45 cm per stride. Stay in a consistent partial squat throughout.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Controlled step pace — roughly 1 step per second.
coaching_cues: Stay low — don't pop up between steps
Push knees out — fight the band
Keep toes forward — don't let feet turn out excessively
